messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tane, a 45-year-old Māori-American chef, came to treatment after several months in which he had been trying to keep his life moving while feeling as though it no longer belonged to him. He had been divorced for two years, living alone in a small apartment near the restaurant where he worked long shifts, and he described himself as someone who had once been defined by his hands: by the speed with which he could break down fish, sharpen a knife, season a sauce by instinct, and run a busy line without missing a beat. The assault happened after a late service, when he accepted a drink from a man he knew only casually through the hospitality scene. He remembered the end of the evening clearly enough to talk about it without much hesitation, but when he tried to place the details in order, the sequence would not settle. He could recall the feeling of being cornered, the confusion of being touched and held down, the sickening realization that he was not going to get out of it, yet when he tried to tell the story from start to finish he found himself losing the order of what happened, jumping ahead, then back, then stopping altogether. He would push the memory away before it was complete, stopping himself halfway through a sentence if he felt the scene becoming too vivid.

In the weeks that followed, Tane found that he could speak about the assault in plain terms if someone asked directly, and he sometimes surprised himself with how easily the words came out. What he could not do was keep the whole memory in view for long. He would begin describing the place, the smell of alcohol, the pressure of the room, and then abruptly cut himself off, as though his mind refused to let him hold the whole thing at once. At the restaurant, certain moments brought it back with force: a coworker standing too close behind him in the tight kitchen, a hand reaching across his back to grab a hot pan, the abrupt closeness of someone blocking his path in the hallway to the walk-in. Those moments did not bring a single clear recollection so much as a jarring sense that the night of the assault had returned in pieces, out of order and unfinished. He noticed himself tensing when a man he did not know well lingered near him after closing, and he became especially uneasy when drink was involved at staff gatherings, where the chatter, laughter, and sudden crowding made him feel exposed in a way he could not fully explain to others.

Tane had come to believe that what had happened had stripped him of the person he had been. He said, with a flatness that made the words heavier, that he was no longer capable of the things that once defined him. The station work that used to feel effortless now left him second-guessing himself, and he found it hard to trust the steadiness of his own body in a room built around heat, knives, and quick movements. Small mistakes at work felt unbearable to him because they seemed to confirm what he already feared: that the assault had taken away his competence, his confidence, and the authority he used to carry in the kitchen. He spoke about his marriage ending in the same breath, saying that it felt as if the trauma had not only interrupted his life but destroyed it altogether. That sense of ruin was not dramatic in the way he described it; it was matter-of-fact, as if he had been forced to accept a damaged version of himself and could not see how to recover what was lost.

Alongside that, he carried a persistent sense of dirtiness that he could not shake. He showered more than once a day at times, scrubbed his skin hard, and still felt contaminated, as though the assault had left something on him that would not wash away. He described the feeling with visible disgust, looking down at his hands as if they no longer belonged to him. This made ordinary contact difficult. He withdrew from casual touch, avoided situations where people might stand close, and kept conversations with colleagues brief when he could. At home he often changed clothes immediately after work and sat alone, trying to settle the uneasy feeling in his body, but the sense of being contaminated remained with him even on quiet evenings. The shame of it also made him pull back socially, and the loneliness that followed was another change in the shape of his days.

By the time he sought help, Tane was no longer trying to pretend the impact had passed. He had reached a point where the memory of the assault, the broken way it came back to him, and the conviction that his life had been ruined were interfering with work and wearing down his remaining sense of control. What brought him in was not a single crisis but the accumulation of moments in the kitchen and outside it that left him feeling cornered, altered, and ashamed. He said he wanted to understand why his body still reacted as if danger were near, and he was most afraid that the man he had been before the assault was gone for good. At the same time, he admitted that he hoped treatment might help him feel clean again, able to work without feeling exposed, and able to tell the story of what happened without having to stop halfway through.
